objectives: Map the major Western + diaspora movement vocabularies.
Locate ballet, modern, jazz, hip-hop, contemporary, improvisation on a technique grid.
Read a choreographer's vocabulary choices as authorial signature.

slides.title: Ballet — five positions, barre, centre, allegro, pointe
slides.body:
A **movement vocabulary** is a codified set of body shapes, transitions, dynamics + counting conventions a dancer can deploy on command. Every form has its own lexicon + grammar; a choreographer picks one or splices several.

**Ballet** — the most documented vocabulary in the West, codified at Louis XIV's Académie Royale de Danse from 1661 (Pierre Beauchamp's five positions). Vocabulary in French because of the 17C French court.

**Five positions of the feet** (Beauchamp ~1700): heels turned out from the hip; toes ~180° apart in classical bias. 1st = heels touching. 2nd = ~shoulder-width apart. 3rd = one heel against arch of other. 4th = stepped apart along the median. 5th = full crossing, heel-to-toe. The whole ballet syllabus is built on entries + exits from these.

**Daily class structure** — universally barre then centre:
- **Barre** (≈45 min). Pliés, tendus, dégagés, ronds de jambe, frappés, fondus, adagio (slow weight-bearing), grands battements, stretches.
- **Centre** (≈30-45 min). Adagio (slow control + balance), pirouettes, petit allegro (small fast jumps — glissade, jeté, assemblé, sissonne), grand allegro (large traveling jumps — grand jeté, saut de chat, tour jeté).
- **Pointe** (women + men, contemporary): vertical balance on the toe-box of a reinforced shoe (developed early 19C; Marie Taglioni in *La Sylphide* 1832).

**Adagio + allegro** are the two great speed registers: adagio = sustained, weight-shared, partnered; allegro = jumped, attacked, accented. Petit vs grand distinguishes amplitude. Every ballet has its mix.

**Schools**: French (Paris Opera — elegance, port de bras), Italian (Cecchetti — articulation), Danish (Bournonville — buoyant petit allegro), Russian (Vaganova — épaulement + plastique), English (RAD), Balanchine (NYCB — speed + off-balance attack). Same five positions; different attack + carriage.

**Notation**: barre exercises traditionally taught by demonstration + counts; full ballets recorded via Stepanov + Labanotation + Benesh + video (P89 L4).

slides.title: Modern, jazz + commercial techniques
slides.body:
**Modern dance** rejected ballet's verticality + turnout. Three foundational American techniques:

**Graham technique** (Martha Graham 1926+). Built on **contraction + release** centered in the pelvis + breath; spirals; falls to floor with full body; pelvic tilts; cupped hands; angular geometry. *Lamentation* (1930) is a single dancer inside a tube of jersey — Graham vocabulary visible as pure stretched + contracting line. Codified through 60+ years of teaching at the Graham School.

**Cunningham technique** (Merce Cunningham 1953+). Erect spine like ballet but with curves, tilts, twists of the torso. Independence of upper + lower body. Sudden changes of direction, no fixed front. Trained on the same 6-count + 8-count meter as ballet but choreographed to chance-determined sequence. Cage influence: silence + sound co-existing.

**Limón / Humphrey technique** (José Limón + Doris Humphrey from 1930s). Fall + recovery. Weight + breath as primary engines. Suspension at the top of every phrase. Less angular than Graham, more flowing.

**Release technique** (postmodern; from 1970s — Mary Fulkerson, Susan Klein, Joan Skinner). Letting muscular tension drain; movement initiated by skeletal alignment + breath rather than muscular set. Foundational to most contemporary training today.

**Jazz dance**: African-diasporic + Broadway + film traditions. Isolations (head, ribs, hips, shoulders move independently of the rest); polyrhythm; grounded turnout-neutral stance; syncopation. **Luigi technique** (Eugene Louis Faccuito; New York 1950s+) — therapeutic jazz developed after a car accident; the dominant commercial-jazz syllabus through to today. **Mattox**, **Cole** + **Fosse** styles each have a vocabulary recognisable in five seconds (P89 L6 + L7).

**Tap**: percussive footwork on a hard floor — body as drum. Single + double time steps, shuffles, flaps, paradiddles, wings. Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson, Gregory Hines, Savion Glover (P89 L6).

**Commercial / theatrical**: stage jazz, music-video choreography, cheer, competition routines. Borrows from ballet + jazz + hip-hop + acrobatics.

slides.title: Hip-hop, contemporary, improvisation + Forsythe technologies
slides.body:
**Hip-hop dance** is a family of African-American + Latino vernacular forms born in the Bronx + Los Angeles from the late 1960s. Major streams:

- **B-boying / breaking** (Bronx, early 1970s — DJ Kool Herc's block parties; Rock Steady Crew). Toprock, downrock (footwork), freezes, power moves (windmill, flare, headspin). Now an Olympic event (Paris 2024 — covered in P89 L8).
- **Locking** (Los Angeles, 1969 — Don 'Campbellock' Campbell). Sharp arrest of motion mid-phrase; points, wrist rolls, splits. Don Campbell's freezes inside funk grooves.
- **Popping** (Fresno + LA, 1970s — Sam 'Boogaloo Sam' Solomon, Skeeter Rabbit + the Electric Boogaloos). Sudden contraction of muscles on the beat = a 'pop'. Boogaloo, tutting, animation, waving, robot.
- **Krumping** (LA, 2000s — Tommy the Clown, Tight Eyez). High-affect, chest-pop, stomp, jab vocabulary.
- **House** (Chicago + NY clubs, 1980s). Lofting, jacking, footwork, floor work to four-on-the-floor house music.
- **Memphis jookin, Chicago footwork, dancehall, voguing** (Harlem ballroom, *Paris Is Burning*).

**Contemporary dance** = post-1980 hybrid technique. Sources include ballet, Graham, Cunningham, release, contact improvisation, somatic practices (Feldenkrais, Alexander, BMC), yoga, capoeira, hip-hop, parkour. No single syllabus — every major company has a house style.

**Improvisation**:
- **Contact improvisation** (Steve Paxton 1972 — *Magnesium*). Two-body weight-sharing, rolling point of contact, falling + catching. Postmodern + somatic origin.
- **Authentic Movement** (Mary Starks Whitehouse). Eyes closed, witnessed.
- **Composition in real time** (Lisa Nelson, Nancy Stark Smith, João Fiadeiro).

**Forsythe Improvisation Technologies** (William Forsythe, late 1990s — CD-ROM 1999). A pedagogical system + interactive media artifact decomposing ballet vocabulary into geometric operations: extruding lines, folding planes, isometries, residues. Dancers given a small vocabulary of operations + improvise on assigned material. Yields choreographies like *One Flat Thing, reproduced* (2000). Forsythe shows that ballet's grammar can be opened up algorithmically without abandoning its skill base.

**Choosing a vocabulary** = authorial signature. Pina Bausch builds from pedestrian gesture + Tanztheater repetition; Crystal Pite from ballet + theatre + ensemble cinema; Bill T. Jones from modern + Black vernacular + text; Akram Khan from Kathak + contemporary. A choreographer's identity is the union of vocabularies they choose + the way they sequence them.

question.question: Identify the source vocabulary in four choreographic samples
question.goal: Given four short descriptions, name the dominant technique + a marker that gave it away.

steps.prompt: Sample A: dancers in pointe shoes, 5th-position sissonnes diagonally upstage, port de bras épaulé, music is Tchaikovsky.

acceptedAnswers: classical ballet — pointe + fifth position + Tchaikovsky

steps.reveal: Classical ballet. Pointe + fifth position + Tchaikovsky orchestration locate it in the Petipa heritage; sissonne + épaulé are Petipa-era ballet vocabulary words. Russian (Vaganova) carriage is implied by the épaulement description.

steps.prompt: Sample B: floorwork with pelvic contractions, cupped hand on diaphragm, fall to the side knees-first, no shoes, breath audible.

acceptedAnswers: Graham technique — contraction + release + cupped hand + breath

steps.reveal: Graham technique. Contraction + release centered in the pelvis + breath; cupped hand against the diaphragm + audible breath are Graham signatures. Floor-work + barefoot + sideways fall further confirm; *Lamentation* (1930) is the canonical reference image.

steps.prompt: Sample C: dancer freezes mid-phrase on beat 2; sharp shoulder pop on beat 4; rolling waist tutting; the body is a sequence of stopped photographs.
hints: Sudden muscular arrests on the beat.
steps.reveal: Popping (with possible locking elements). Sudden contraction of muscles on the beat = pop. Lineage: Boogaloo Sam + Skeeter Rabbit + the Electric Boogaloos (Fresno + LA 1970s). Locking (Don Campbell, LA 1969) would emphasise the freeze + wrist-roll + point. Both are funk-styles; both come from Black + Latino vernacular street dance.

steps.prompt: Sample D: two dancers in physical contact; weight rolls from shoulder to back to hip across both bodies; one lifts the other onto the spine without preparation; eyes soft, no music or ambient texture only.
steps.reveal: Contact improvisation, invented by Steve Paxton in 1972 (*Magnesium*). Continuous weight-sharing through a rolling point of contact; falling + catching as fundamental skill. Postmodern origin (Judson lineage). Now embedded in most contemporary-dance training worldwide.

question.question: Which best characterises William Forsythe's Improvisation Technologies (late 1990s)?
options: A pedagogical system + interactive CD-ROM that decomposes ballet vocabulary into geometric operations (line extrusion, plane folding, isometry, residue) which dancers then improvise from. Forsythe demonstrates that classical ballet's grammar can be opened up algorithmically — yielding ensemble works like *One Flat Thing, reproduced* (2000) — without abandoning the skill base of pointe + turnout + adagio. It is one of the first computer-mediated pedagogies in dance; influential on contemporary training globally + on later digital + AI choreography (P89 L4 + L8).
question.explanation: Forsythe's Improvisation Technologies (CD-ROM 1999) is a pedagogical decomposition of ballet into geometric operations from which dancers improvise. Yielded *One Flat Thing, reproduced* (2000). First computer-mediated dance pedagogy; influence reaches contemporary training + later AI choreography (P89 L8).
hints: Forsythe didn't invent a notation — Laban + Benesh + Eshkol already had those.
question.workedSolution: Forsythe + Frankfurt Ballet collaborators built Improvisation Technologies as both a teaching method + a CD-ROM (1999). Ballet vocabulary is decomposed into geometric operations on the body in space — extruding a line through the spine, folding a plane through the elbow, leaving a 'residue' after a movement ends — which dancers recombine in real time. *One Flat Thing, reproduced* (2000) is the most visible product. The method is the first major computer-mediated pedagogy in dance + a direct ancestor of later digital + AI choreography (P89 L8).

question.question: Casting + training for a hybrid commission
question.prompt: A presenter commissions you to make a 25-minute work that fuses Petipa-era classical ballet vocabulary with popping. You have 8 dancers + 6 weeks of rehearsal. Half are classically trained ballet dancers; half are battle-credentialed poppers. Describe (a) your first-week training plan that lets each group acquire a working competence in the other's vocabulary; (b) the one or two specific movement-grammar collisions you will exploit choreographically (e.g. fifth-position relevé into a freeze); (c) the casting problem you must solve + how (lifts, partnering, costume + footwear, injury risk).

question.question: An adagio at ♩ = 60 BPM lasts 4 minutes. A petit allegro at ♩ = 144 BPM has the same number of beats as the adagio. How long (in seconds) is the petit allegro?

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain why a choreographer's choice of movement vocabulary is an authorial decision — not a neutral technical baseline. Cite three specific choreographer-vocabulary pairings + the historical lineage of each.
question.rubric: Should articulate: vocabulary carries history + body politics + audience association; choosing one is already a statement. Three pairings, e.g.: (1) Petipa with classical ballet — Imperial Russian Mariinsky pedagogy, turnout, pointe, Tchaikovsky-era musicality; (2) Martha Graham with contraction-release — pelvis-centered American modern, Denishawn lineage, mythic-psychological themes; (3) Crystal Pite with ballet + theatre + ensemble — Forsythe + William Pita lineage, cinematic mass formations; or alternates (Bill T. Jones with modern + Black vernacular + text; Akram Khan with Kathak + contemporary). Should note that choosing pedestrian gesture (Bausch, Rainer) or hip-hop battle vocabulary (Crazy Legs, Skeeter Rabbit) is equally authorial — even refusing a vocabulary is a choice. Vocabulary = the choreographer's signature.
